messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The blast that tore through the downtown market still lives in Malik’s bones. He remembers the sudden vacuum of air, the deafening crack, and the suffocating smoke that coated his tongue. His colleagues were gone in an instant, dragged under rubble that had been solid moments before. That chaotic suffocation and the unpredictable violence are why the smell of burnt rubber now locks his chest, and why the sudden clatter of a dropped fabric bolt in his tailor shop feels like another detonation. In the weeks that followed, the event refused to settle. There were entire stretches of the aftermath he simply could not remember, no matter how hard he pressed his fingers to his temples. When fragments did surface, they played on a relentless loop, vivid and unyielding. Yet, his lingering conviction that he was fundamentally weak and that he belonged nowhere actively shaped how those memories surfaced; because he believed he had failed to protect himself and his community, his mind began to fracture the trauma into emotionless, detached recollections, as if he were merely an observer of a stranger’s tragedy. The replaying footage itself also wired his nervous system into a permanent state of alert. Within months, Malik found himself scanning every doorway the moment he stepped into a space, his eyes darting to fire escapes and side doors before he even reached the counter. He refused to sit facing the floor, pressing his spine firmly against the interior wall so he could watch the street. The constant need to monitor the perimeter left him exhausted, but the relief of having an unobstructed view was the only thing that kept the panic at bay. Those corrosive beliefs and the relentless alertness soon dictated how he survived each day. Because he no longer trusted his own judgment to keep himself safe, Malik began avoiding any conversation that looked toward the horizon, convinced that preparing for tomorrow was pointless. The exhausting hypervigilance of scanning exits and pressing his back to the wall left him with no emotional bandwidth, so he gravitated toward his phone, scrolling through games and videos for hours to keep his mind occupied. The strategy worked until the isolation bred resentment, and he would deliberately pick fights with delivery drivers or customers, manufacturing drama to outrun the quiet. When the shop grew quiet and the intrusive memories threatened to surface, that same self-doubt pushed him toward these distractions. Yet the unrelenting threat monitoring only fed his original convictions; the more he scanned for danger and found it everywhere, the more certain he became that he belonged nowhere, and that he was fundamentally inadequate. He stopped making plans for the year ahead, convinced that the future could be erased in a single breath. The tension between his hyperawareness of the present and his conviction that he was fundamentally broken only intensified; the more he scanned for danger, the more his memories replayed, and the more he felt his own fragility, driving him back to his screens and his arguments, tightening the loop that kept him trapped. Now, at thirty-three, the exhaustion has finally eclipsed the numbness. The recent loss of a long-term client, who cited his erratic behavior and withdrawn nature as the reason for taking his work elsewhere, pushed Malik to the edge. He walked into the clinic today hoping someone might finally help him untangle the noise in his head. He is terrified that the help will come too late to save his livelihood, but he holds onto the faint hope that he might learn to trust himself again.
